questions.prompt: What does FOMO mean in investing?
choices: Fear Of Missing Out — rushing to buy because everyone else seems to be getting rich
A low-fee index fund
A government program that insures your losses
The fee a broker charges to sell a stock
questions.explanation: FOMO pushes people to buy after a price has already soared, often right near the top.

questions.prompt: Panic-selling during a market drop turns a temporary paper loss into a permanent, real one.
questions.explanation: A loss on paper only becomes real when you sell — holding gives prices a chance to recover.

questions.prompt: Which are signs that FOMO — not real analysis — is driving your decision? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: A stock is all over your feed and 'everyone' seems to own it
You feel a rush of urgency to buy right now before you miss out
You read the company's financials and decided the price was fair
You're scared of being the only one left out of the gains
questions.explanation: FOMO feels urgent and social; real analysis is calm and based on facts, not on the crowd.

questions.prompt: Put the classic FOMO trap in order, from start to painful finish.
items: A stock's price skyrockets and fills your feed
You feel you're missing out and buy near the peak
The hype fades and the price falls
You panic-sell at a loss
questions.explanation: Buying on hype and selling on fear is the buy-high, sell-low trap in action.

questions.prompt: A stock you own drops 20% on scary headlines, but nothing about the actual business changed. The emotionally-smart move is usually to:
choices: Stick to your plan and avoid selling out of fear
Immediately sell everything to stop the pain
Borrow money to buy a huge amount right now
Refresh the price every five minutes all day
questions.explanation: Reacting to fear locks in losses; a plan keeps emotion from making the decision for you.

questions.prompt: The best time to decide how you'll react to a crash is before it happens, while you're calm.
questions.explanation: Deciding your rules in advance keeps panic from choosing for you in the moment.

questions.prompt: 'Buy high, sell low' is the opposite of good investing. Which emotions most often cause it?
choices: Greed/FOMO when buying, and fear/panic when selling
Boredom when buying, and pride when selling
Curiosity when buying, and gratitude when selling
Patience when buying, and calm when selling
questions.explanation: Greed tempts you to buy at the top; fear tempts you to sell at the bottom.

questions.prompt: Match each bias to its meaning.
pairs: Loss aversion
Losses hurt about twice as much as equal gains feel good
Anchoring
Fixating on one number, like the price you paid, when judging value
Confirmation bias
Only seeking out information that agrees with what you already believe
Herd mentality
Doing what the crowd does instead of thinking for yourself
questions.explanation: Naming a bias is the first step to catching yourself doing it.

questions.prompt: You refuse to sell a losing stock 'until it gets back to what I paid for it.' Which bias is this?
choices: Anchoring to your purchase price
Herd mentality
Confirmation bias
Diversification
questions.explanation: The market doesn't care what you paid; anchoring to that number clouds your judgment.

questions.prompt: Loss aversion means the pain of losing $100 usually feels stronger than the joy of gaining $100.
questions.explanation: Because losses sting more, people often sell winners too early and cling to losers too long.

questions.prompt: Sort each behavior into the bias it shows.
items: Only reading articles that praise a stock you own
Confirmation bias
Buying a coin because your whole group chat is buying it
Herd mentality
Ignoring a report that lists risks you'd rather not see
Confirmation bias
Selling in a panic just because everyone else is selling
Herd mentality
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias filters your information; herd mentality copies the crowd.

questions.prompt: The best defense against confirmation bias is to:
choices: Actively look for solid arguments against your own idea
Only follow people who already agree with you
Avoid reading anything at all
Buy more of a stock every time it drops
questions.explanation: Seeking out the other side stress-tests your idea before your money has to.

questions.prompt: Which of these show herd mentality? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Buying a stock only because it's trending and everyone's talking about it
Selling because you see everyone else panic-selling
Buying after researching the company and deciding it's a fair price
Piling into a meme coin so you won't feel left out
questions.explanation: Herd mentality is letting the crowd — not your own analysis — make the call.

questions.prompt: Anchoring can trick you into thinking a stock is 'cheap' just because it's lower than its all-time high.
questions.explanation: A lower price isn't automatically a bargain; the business's actual value is what matters.

questions.prompt: An investment 'guarantees' you'll double your money in a month with 'zero risk.' This is:
choices: A major red flag — real investments never guarantee high returns with no risk
A normal, safe opportunity you should jump on
Proof the investment is government-regulated
A sign of a well-diversified portfolio
questions.explanation: Higher returns always come with higher risk, so 'guaranteed' big returns are a classic scam signal.

questions.prompt: In a Ponzi scheme, early investors are paid with money from new investors — not from real profits.
questions.explanation: It collapses the moment new money slows, and most people end up losing everything.

questions.prompt: In a 'pump-and-dump,' scammers hype a cheap stock or coin to push the price up, and then:
choices: Sell their own shares at the top, crashing the price for everyone else
Donate all the profits to charity
Hold forever and never sell
Report themselves to regulators
questions.explanation: The organizers dump their shares on the hype, leaving latecomers holding the losses.

questions.prompt: Which are red flags of a likely scam? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Promises of guaranteed, unusually high returns
High pressure to 'act now' before you can think or research
A boring, low-cost index fund with clear disclosures
Being told to recruit friends to earn bigger payouts
questions.explanation: Guarantees, urgency, and recruit-your-friends schemes are classic warning signs.

questions.prompt: Sort each into a scam red flag or a healthy sign.
items: 'Guaranteed' 500% returns
Red flag
Clear, public financial statements
Healthy sign
Pressure to invest before you can research
Red flag
A regulated fund with transparent fees
Healthy sign
questions.explanation: Transparency is healthy; secrecy, guarantees, and pressure are red flags.

questions.prompt: A paid promotion from an influencer counts as solid financial research.
questions.explanation: Paid promos are advertising, not analysis — the promoter is being paid to say nice things.

questions.prompt: A celebrity you follow is paid to promote a new crypto token. Before buying, you should:
choices: Do your own research — a paid endorsement isn't evidence the token is good
Buy immediately because they're famous and trustworthy
Invest your whole savings to show support
Assume it's guaranteed to rise because a celebrity likes it
questions.explanation: Fame isn't expertise, and paid promos come with a built-in conflict of interest.

questions.prompt: Automating a set investment every payday (dollar-cost averaging) helps you:
choices: Invest consistently without letting emotions or timing get in the way
Guarantee you always buy at the lowest possible price
Avoid ever paying any taxes
Beat the market every single year
questions.explanation: Automatic, regular investing removes the temptation to time the market on emotion.

questions.prompt: You automate investing $150 every month. How many dollars is that over one year?
questions.explanation: $150 x 12 months = $1,800 invested automatically.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of a healthy 'rules before you invest' habit in order.
items: Write down your goal and your rules while calm
Automate regular contributions
Check your portfolio on a set schedule, not constantly
Follow your written rules instead of your mood
questions.explanation: Deciding rules in advance and automating them keeps emotion out of the driver's seat.

questions.prompt: Checking your portfolio every few minutes tends to increase stress and lead to worse decisions.
questions.explanation: Constant checking amplifies emotion; a calm, scheduled review is healthier and usually smarter.

questions.prompt: Writing an 'investing rulebook' before you buy is helpful mainly because:
choices: Calm, pre-set rules protect you from emotional decisions later
It guarantees you'll never lose money
It lets you skip doing any research
It makes your returns tax-free
questions.explanation: Rules written in a calm moment act as guardrails when fear or greed hit later.

questions.prompt: Which of these are good investing habits? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Automating contributions so you invest before you can spend it
Reviewing your portfolio on a set schedule, like quarterly
Writing down your plan and rules ahead of time
Trading impulsively every time you see a scary headline
questions.explanation: Automation, scheduled reviews, and written rules build discipline; impulsive trading breaks it.

questions.prompt: If you review your portfolio once every 3 months, how many times do you check it in a year?
questions.explanation: 12 months / 3 = 4 scheduled reviews per year — calm and consistent.

questions.prompt: The saying 'time in the market beats timing the market' means:
choices: Staying invested over the long run usually beats jumping in and out
You should only invest for a single day at a time
The best investors trade many times per hour
You must predict every crash to succeed
questions.explanation: Since no one reliably times the market, patient long-term investing tends to win.

questions.prompt: Missing just a handful of the market's best days can drastically lower your long-term returns.
questions.explanation: The biggest up-days often come right after big drops, so jumping out risks missing the rebound.

questions.prompt: 'Buy-and-hold' investing means:
choices: Buying quality investments and holding them for years through the ups and downs
Selling everything the moment prices dip
Buying and selling the same stock every day
Only holding cash and never investing
questions.explanation: Buy-and-hold lets compounding work and cuts down on emotional, costly trading.

questions.prompt: An investor's money grows about 10% per year. Using the Rule of 72, roughly how many years until it doubles?
questions.explanation: The Rule of 72 says 72 / 10 is about 7.2 years to double.

questions.prompt: Match each mindset to the investor it describes.
pairs: Patient long-term investor
Buys quality and holds for years, ignoring daily noise
Panic trader
Sells in fear every time the market dips
Market timer
Tries (and usually fails) to guess the perfect moment to buy and sell
FOMO chaser
Piles into whatever is hot right now, near its peak
questions.explanation: The calm, patient approach is the one that most reliably builds wealth over time.

questions.prompt: Because the stock market has trended upward over the long run, staying invested has historically rewarded patience.
questions.explanation: Despite crashes along the way, long-term investors have historically been rewarded for holding.

questions.prompt: Compounding rewards long-term investors most because:
choices: Your gains start earning their own gains, snowballing over many years
The government adds free money each year
Stocks can only ever go up
Short-term trading always earns more
questions.explanation: Given time, compounding turns steady growth into a snowball — the longer you wait, the bigger it gets.

questions.prompt: FOMO most often leads investors to:
choices: Buy near the top, after a price has already surged on hype
Buy low and sell high automatically
Avoid the stock market entirely
Diversify across many different assets
questions.explanation: FOMO strikes after prices soar, tempting you to buy right before the hype fades.

questions.prompt: Panic-selling in a crash locks in your losses instead of giving prices a chance to recover.
questions.explanation: A paper loss only becomes permanent once you actually sell.

questions.prompt: Match each bias to its meaning.
pairs: Loss aversion
Losses feel worse than equal gains feel good
Anchoring
Over-fixating on one number, like the price you paid
Confirmation bias
Only seeking information that agrees with you
Herd mentality
Copying the crowd instead of thinking independently
questions.explanation: Spotting a bias by name helps you avoid falling into its trap.

questions.prompt: Which of these are red flags of an investment scam? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: 'Guaranteed' high returns with no risk
Pressure to act immediately
Transparent fees and public financial statements
Rewards for recruiting new investors
questions.explanation: Guarantees, urgency, and recruitment are classic scam signals; transparency is a good sign.

questions.prompt: A paid influencer promotion is a reliable substitute for doing your own research.
questions.explanation: Paid promos are ads with a built-in conflict of interest, not real analysis.

questions.prompt: Sort each into a smart habit or an emotional trap.
items: Automating monthly contributions
Smart habit
Panic-selling on scary headlines
Emotional trap
Reviewing your portfolio on a set schedule
Smart habit
Chasing whatever is trending out of FOMO
Emotional trap
questions.explanation: Discipline and automation build wealth; emotional reactions erode it.

questions.prompt: You automate $200 a month. How many dollars do you invest over a full year?
Put this emotional buy-high, sell-low cycle in order.
items: Hype and FOMO push you to buy near the top
The market drops and headlines turn scary
Fear pushes you to panic-sell at a loss
You miss the rebound that follows
questions.explanation: Emotion makes investors buy high and sell low — the exact opposite of the goal.

questions.prompt: 'Time in the market beats timing the market' teaches you to:
choices: Stay invested for the long run rather than jumping in and out
Trade as often as you possibly can
Only invest for one day at a time
Sell everything before every dip
questions.explanation: Since timing the market reliably is nearly impossible, patience usually wins.

questions.prompt: Which statement is TRUE?
choices: A Ponzi scheme pays old investors with new investors' money and eventually collapses
Guaranteed high returns with zero risk are a sign of a safe investment
Herd mentality means always thinking independently
Panic-selling is the best response to a market dip
questions.explanation: Ponzi schemes have no real profits — they run on new money until it dries up.
